page.title: Day 4 against Neave's manual
page.standfirst_html: Every flag the comparator raised for Day 4, adjudicated against G.Day.4.09Jan20.pdf — the extracted text for wording, and thirteen page images for emphasis, colour and block structure. Day 4 is in materially worse shape than any day adjudicated so far. Its clean match rate is 57%, and the defects are not the wrong-page-number kind that dominated Days 9 and 11: seven passages are missing from the site outright, four blocks of text sit in the wrong place, and three sentences appear on the site that are in no source at all. The two that matter most are invisible to every automated check. Point 1's entire “Obsession With Quality” section is a verbatim copy of Point 3's — it argues about mass inspection and quotes a phrase that occurs only in Point 3's statement — so a learner working the First Project is linking Point 1 to a foundation using the wrong Point's argument. And Activity 4–a's “see the Appendix” link points into the Day 3 appendix, landing the reader mid-way through an unrelated story, while the Day 4 appendix on the other side already implements the return trip correctly. Three findings also reverse Neave's meaning rather than blur it: “hardly” read as “merely”, an emphasis on tools “well beyond the control chart” read as “particularly the control chart”, and Pause for Thought 4–c's revealed answer giving a different answer from the one Neave gives. #676's three fixes to The First Project were re-verified against the page images and are correct; this pass proposes nothing on them, and one new defect on the same page that #676 did not catch.

sections.note_html: Ordered by source page. Thirty are marked critical — by a distance the heaviest load of any pass in this wave. Seven are passages missing from the site outright, four are text pasted from the wrong place (including Point 1's entire “Obsession With Quality” section, which is Point 3's), three are sentences with no source at all, and one is a cross-reference that sends the reader into the Day 3 appendix.

items.source_html: You may recall that we have already referred <mark class='src'>during</mark> “The Deming Story” to a video made in 1984 …
items.site_html: You may recall that we have already referred <mark class='gone'>in</mark> "The Deming Story" to a video made in 1984 …
items.proposal: You may recall that we have already referred during "The Deming Story" to a video made in 1984 which shows Dr Deming speaking passionately about the dangers of the five Deadly Diseases (see [Day 1 pages 37–38](../day-01/11-deming-story.qmd#sec-page37)), so his awareness of them and of the harm they cause clearly grew rapidly in his mind during the two years after the earlier book was published.
items.evidence_html: Page image, printed p1: “referred during ‘The Deming Story’”. Small, but “during” places the reference in the session; “in” places it in the text.

items.source_html: … because people would keep asking me awkward questions that I couldn’t answer! Thinking hard about the matter (as one would), I began to realise that merely considering the 14 Points one by one, important although that had to be, was just not sufficient. At that time I really had little appreciation of the Deming philosophy as a system, in the sense in which we have begun to use that word. … worth talking about in their own right—but clearly their prime purpose and role is to help form the big picture.
items.site_html: … because people would keep asking me awkward questions <mark class='gone'>about them!</mark> Thinking hard about the matter (<mark class='gone'>as I always do</mark>), I began to realise that <mark class='gone'>merely consulting individual pieces of the Deming philosophy as a system</mark>, in the sense in which we have begun to use that word. … worth talking about in their own right—but <mark class='gone'>they clearly their prime purpose</mark> and role is to help form the big picture.
items.proposal: In those early seminars, I soon realised I must be getting something wrong concerning the 14 Points—because people would keep asking me awkward questions that I couldn't answer! Thinking hard about the matter (as one would), I began to realise that merely considering the 14 Points one by one, important although that had to be, was just not sufficient. At that time I really had little appreciation of the Deming philosophy as a *system*, in the sense in which we have begun to use that word. To put it metaphorically, I was talking about the individual pieces of a jigsaw without trying to fit the pieces together. No wonder that I was unable to answer my delegates' questions! Perhaps it is a comment on the attractive nature of Dr Deming's material that individual pieces of the jigsaw are *worth* talking about in their own right—but clearly their prime purpose and role is to help form the big picture.
items.evidence_html: Four defects in one paragraph, all confirmed on the page image (printed p2). The serious one is the third: a whole sentence is gone and the two either side of it are fused into a clause with no main verb — “I began to realise that merely consulting individual pieces of the Deming philosophy as a system, in the sense in which we have begun to use that word.” reads as a sentence fragment on the live site. The fourth is a stray inserted they that breaks the grammar a second time. The proposal also restores the source's italics on system and worth.

items.source_html: … which are largely based on those which I included in my handouts for those early seminars, it is clear that I saw a few links between the various Points—but not many. It is almost as if I regarded such links as happy coincidences rather than as an essential feature of their contents. However, as I thought about some of the awkward questions from delegates, I began to see that it was just those very links to other matters about which Dr Deming was also talking and writing that showed the way to answer those questions.
items.site_html: … which are largely based on those which I included in <mark class='gone'>my earlier materials</mark>, it is almost as if I regarded such links as happy coincidences rather than as an essential feature of their <mark class='gone'>content</mark>. However, as <mark class='gone'>I began to think about some awkward questions from my delegates</mark>, I began to see that it was just those very links to other matters about which Dr Deming was also talking <mark class='gone'>that showed the power of the work.</mark>
items.proposal: Nowadays, as I re-read my comments on the 14 Points in *DemDim* Chapter 3, which are largely based on those which I included in my handouts for those early seminars, it is clear that I saw a *few* links between the various Points—but not many. It is almost as if I regarded such links as happy coincidences rather than as an essential feature of their contents. However, as I thought about some of the awkward questions from delegates, I began to see that it was just those very links to other matters about which Dr Deming was also talking and writing that showed the way to answer those questions. And this encouraged me to search for a more fruitful way of finding those links and understanding them—and thus understanding more of what Dr Deming was teaching, and why—rather better than had so far been the case.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p2. An entire sentence is missing (“it is clear that I saw a few links between the various Points—but not many”), and the paragraph's own point is inverted by its loss: the site now has “it is almost as if I regarded such links as happy coincidences” with no preceding claim that there were few links. The last defect is substantive too — “showed the way to answer those questions” is the sentence's payoff (it closes the loop with the awkward questions two paragraphs up); “showed the power of the work” does not.

items.source_html: On page 11 you will see <mark class='src'>their</mark> more detailed version of the Triangle …
items.site_html: On page 11 you will see <mark class='gone'>the</mark> more detailed version of the Triangle …
items.proposal: In fact, the people at Joiner Associates used only *six* words, with the top of the Triangle being condensed to just "Quality". However, that struck me as being rather too nebulous. On [page 11, in the Joiner Triangle chapter](02-the-joiner-triangle.qmd#sec-page11) you will see their more detailed version of the Triangle which shows some of the items to be included under each of the three headings.
items.evidence_html: Printed p2. “their” attributes the expanded Triangle to Joiner Associates, which is the whole subject of the sentence before it, and is what the figure on printed p11 is captioned as on the site. “the” loses the attribution.

items.source_html: It is something of which I became increasingly aware in Dr Deming’s work—<mark class='src'>but also something of which I saw little during the more academic pursuits in the first half of my career life.</mark> In academia it seems as if one has to come up with pretty complicated things in order to be regarded as profound!
items.site_html: It is something of which I became increasingly aware in Dr Deming's work—<mark class='gone'>the Deming philosophy.</mark> In academia it seems as if one has to come up with pretty complicated things in order to be regarded as profound!
items.proposal: I have already emphasised this combination of *simple* and *profound* with regard to the Red Beads Experiment. It is something of which I became increasingly aware in Dr Deming's work—but also something of which I saw little during the more academic pursuits in the first half of my career life. In academia it seems as if one has to come up with pretty complicated things in order to be regarded as profound!
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p3. The clause the site dropped is what sets up the next sentence: without “I saw little of it during the more academic pursuits in the first half of my career life”, the jump to “In academia it seems as if…” has nothing to attach to, and the substituted “the Deming philosophy” is a tautology after “in Dr Deming's work”.

items.site_html: <mark class='gone'>So the current work will also be</mark> excellent preparation for that later stage.
items.proposal: So the current work will also be excellent preparation for that later stage. → Your current work will therefore be excellent preparation for that later stage.
items.evidence_html: Printed p3. “therefore” carries the inference from the sentence before (the overlap with Deming's own four foundations); “also” makes it an unrelated addition.

items.source_html: I will then expand further on “Obsession With Quality”, <mark class='src'>because I’m well aware of some of the doubts and arguments that might arise concerning that concept</mark>, especially concerning my sharper focus there compared with the original.

items.proposal: But, before that, let us spend the rest of this morning studying the Joiner Triangle's three foundations. The first thing for you to do will be to read my brief discussion in *DemDim*—just over five pages. After that, I shall get you to work on the "Scientific Approach" and "All One Team". items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p3. The site's version is not a paraphrase but a broken sentence — “after we complete” has no object, and “I'm very much aware of the concept” loses the reason Neave gives for the expansion, which is that readers will have doubts about it.

items.source_html: its “culture”, its <mark class='src'>values</mark> and principles, the reward and punishment mechanisms …
items.site_html: its "culture", its <mark class='gone'>rules</mark> and principles, the reward and punishment mechanisms …
items.proposal: … a host of them which relate directly to the company or organisation as a whole: its "culture", its values and principles, the reward and punishment mechanisms, the nourishment or discouragement of innovation …
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p4: “its values and principles”. This one slipped past the comparator because the paragraph scored as a clean match overall. It matters: the list is of common causes in the system, and “values” names something cultural, while “rules” names something procedural — and “rules and principles” also reads oddly next to “reward and punishment mechanisms”, which is the procedural item.

items.site_html: Again consider situations familiar to you, <mark class='gone'>whether in your family</mark>, perhaps in clubs or societies with which you are involved.

What would be some of the losses?</mark>

Are you aware of anything or any things that might, now or in the future, harm or even destroy that All One Team relationship? What would be some of the losses?
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p6. Three source questions have been spliced into two, and both are nonsense as they stand: “gains that might, now or in the future, have been obtained”, and “anything or any things that would be some of the losses”. The question the splice destroyed — what might harm or even destroy the All One Team relationship — is the substantive half of the If-Yes branch, and the workbook field beneath it still promises “what gains or losses result”.

items.source_html: “a number of companies set their own specifications based on what they think a very varied market will find acceptable.”
items.site_html: "a number of companies set their own specifications based on what they think <mark class='gone'>a wide variety of customers</mark> will find acceptable."
items.proposal: Further, "a number of companies set their own specifications based on what they *think* a very varied market will find acceptable. Often this is an R&D Department which is far removed from the practicalities of production" (my thanks to Dr Jackie Graham for this observation).
items.evidence_html: Printed p8 image. This is inside a quotation Neave attributes to Dr Jackie Graham, so the site is putting words in a named third party's mouth. “a very varied market” and “a wide variety of customers” are not the same claim either — the first is about the spread of a market, the second about a count of customers. The source also italicises think.

items.source_html: … there is often a tendency to breathe a sigh of relief <mark class='src'>(“We’ve made it!”) and for the improvement effort to stagnate</mark>—at least for the time being.
items.site_html: … there is often a tendency to breathe a sigh of relief<mark class='gone'>—one of the most natural things in the world</mark> for the time being.
items.proposal: Two particular problems with this attitude to quality are as follows (wherever the specifications originate). First, having worked to reach the standard or target or specification, etc, there is often a tendency to breathe a sigh of relief ("We've made it!") and for the improvement effort to stagnate—at least for the time being.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p8. The site drops the two things that make this the first of two particular problems: Neave's quoted “We've made it!” and, crucially, “and for the improvement effort to stagnate” — the actual problem. What replaces it (“one of the most natural things in the world”) appears nowhere in the source and excuses the behaviour the paragraph is criticising.

items.source_html: Deming often spoke disparagingly about “fudging figures” <mark class='src'>by means such as redefining methods of measurement or of counting—e.g.</mark> what exactly qualifies for descriptions such as “punctual” or “defective”?
items.site_html: Deming often spoke disparagingly about "fudging figures" <mark class='gone'>(to be discussed later) as redefining methods of measurement—so</mark> what exactly qualifies for descriptions such as "punctual" or "defective"?
items.proposal: Deming often spoke disparagingly about "fudging figures" by means such as redefining methods of measurement or of counting—e.g. what exactly qualifies for descriptions such as "punctual" or "defective"? (The work on operational definitions on Day 11 will be very relevant here.)
items.evidence_html: Printed p8. “or of counting” is dropped, and “punctual”/“defective” are counting definitions, not measurement ones — so the examples no longer match the clause they illustrate. “(to be discussed later)” is not in the source, and duplicates the parenthesis at the end of the same sentence. The proposal also marks “fudging figures” as a .deming_quote, which is what the source's blue does (see the emphasis group).

items.source_html: Of course, he is not suggesting that there’s <mark class='src'>no need to bother to meet specifications!</mark>
items.site_html: Of course, he is not suggesting that there's <mark class='gone'>nothing to be gained from meeting specifications!</mark>
items.proposal: Of course, he is not suggesting that there's no need to bother to meet specifications!
items.evidence_html: Printed p8 image. The two say different things. The source's concession is about effort (“you still have to meet them”); the site's is about benefit (“meeting them still gains you something”). Since the paragraph's job is to pre-empt readers who find the teaching challenging, the concession Neave actually makes is the one that answers the objection.

items.source_html: Even then, this could hardly be referred to as an obsession with quality!
items.site_html: Even then, this could <mark class='gone'>merely</mark> be referred to as an obsession with quality<mark class='gone'>.</mark>
items.proposal: Even then, this could hardly be referred to as an *obsession* with quality! "Obsession" is much more indicative of *continual* improvement, making quality a "way of life", etc—whether or not there appears to be any vital and immediate *need* to do so.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p8. “hardly” and “merely” point opposite ways, and the next sentence settles which Neave meant: “‘Obsession’ is much more indicative of continual improvement … whether or not there appears to be any vital and immediate need” only follows from “hardly”. As it stands the site says defensive quality improvement is an obsession with quality and then immediately argues that it isn't. The source also italicises obsession and ends on an exclamation mark.

items.source_html:
A previous example was seen in my discussion on Pause for Thought 1–c (Appendix page 6) where I alluded to the damaging confusion with “quality assurance”. Considerations of “cost of quality”, for instance, guide one to think in terms of how far it is “cost-effective” to improve quality, with the impression that there is some optimum stage at which to stop improving quality. (Do you think the Japanese “economic miracle” would have happened if they had thought like that?) However if, in Activity 4–a, you thought seriously about Lloyd Nelson’s “unknown and unknowable” figures … the weakness of “cost of quality” considerations becomes very evident. (In connection with this, also look out tomorrow for the fifth of the Deadly Diseases.) A further massive issue … is the great savings that are often made as a result of reducing variation …

An interesting related topic … is COPQ: the cost of poor quality. I have had examples described to me where the yearly COPQ was found to exceed the annual profits!

Deming had a great question to ask of those who were keen on “Zero Defects” and “Right First Time”, etc. It was “By what method?”. I do not recall him ever getting much of a reply.
items.site_html: A previous example was seen in my discussion on Pause for Thought 1–c ([Appendix page 6]), where <mark class='gone'>I argued that this confusion over measurement of quality causes the impression that there is some optimum place at which to stop improving quality. (Do you think this was being adopted, whether or not it has any connection with what Deming was teaching?)</mark>
items.proposal: This is another situation where some teaching about quality from other sources is directly obstructive to Deming's teaching. A previous example was seen in my discussion on Pause for Thought 1–c ([Appendix page 6](../../appendix/01-day-1.qmd#sec-page6)) where I alluded to the damaging confusion with "quality assurance". Considerations of "cost of quality", for instance, guide one to think in terms of how far it is "cost-effective" to improve quality, with the impression that there is some optimum stage at which to *stop* improving quality. (Do you think the Japanese "economic miracle" would have happened if they had thought like that?) However if, in Activity 4–a, you thought seriously about Lloyd Nelson's "unknown and unknowable" figures which he claimed were the "most important" for the organisation, the weakness of "cost of quality" considerations becomes very evident. (In connection with this, also look out tomorrow for the fifth of the Deadly Diseases.) A further massive issue which is ignored in such primitive considerations is the great *savings* that are often made as a result of reducing variation, indicated e.g. in the top half of Deming's Chain Reaction (*DemDim* page 33)—and remind yourself about what that leads to in the bottom half! An interesting related topic which is popular in some areas of industry is COPQ: the cost of *poor* quality. I have had examples described to me where the yearly COPQ was found to exceed the annual profits! Deming had a great question to ask of those who were keen on "Zero Defects" and "Right First Time", etc. It was "By what method?". I do not recall him ever getting much of a reply.
items.evidence_html: The largest loss in Day 4. The page image (printed p8) shows three indented paragraphs; the site keeps one sentence and a fragment of another. Gone: the “quality assurance” confusion this sentence is about, the whole cost-of-quality argument, the Japanese economic miracle aside, the call-back to Activity 4–a and Lloyd Nelson, the forward pointer to tomorrow's fifth Deadly Disease, the savings-from-reducing-variation point, all of COPQ, and Deming's “By what method?”. What remains is also wrong on its own terms: the site attributes to Pause for Thought 1–c an argument about “measurement of quality” that Neave did not make there, and the trailing parenthesis — “(Do you think this was being adopted, whether or not it has any connection with what Deming was teaching?)” — is a splice of words from printed p12, four pages later (see D4-28).

items.site_html: Both appear on <mark class='gone'>printed p8</mark>, inside the “Obsession With Quality” author's note, four pages before the discussion they belong to.

items.evidence_html: Both page images settle this. Printed p12 has “I recall two occasions in four-day seminars …” as an indented note immediately after the tools paragraph, and “However, as you have seen, Brian did also include …” as body text immediately after that; printed p8 has neither. This is the class of defect the validator's module docstring says it cannot see: text pasted in the wrong place scores a perfect match against its true origin. On the site the QFD anecdote currently sits in a note about conformance to specifications, where nothing has yet mentioned tools — and the “as you have seen” in the second paragraph refers forward to a Triangle the reader will not meet for another four pages.

items.evidence_html: Printed p9 image. The site asks a different question from the one its own reveal answers, and asks the learner to explain how he decided he had done it better — which presupposes a replacement the source's answer does not give (see D4-22).

items.source_html: It was “Capture the market”—with its implication of putting others out of business. In the interests of the “big system”, he later clarified (e.g. in The Deming of America) that his preference was instead for expansion of the market by diversification and innovation—with obvious advantages for both suppliers and customers.

items.proposal: It was "Capture the market"—with its implication of putting others out of business. In the interests of the "big system", he later clarified (e.g. in The Deming of America) that his preference was instead for expansion of the market by diversification and innovation—with obvious advantages for both suppliers and customers.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p9: the pink answer panel says what the proposal says. The site's answer is a different claim about Deming, unsupported by the source, and it is also the wrong shape for the page — “Delight the customer” is Scholtes and Hacquebord's Quality Guideline 1, which the site itself quotes as such three paragraphs later under the very next heading. A learner who writes down the correct answer will be told they got it wrong.

items.source_html: Now, a loud word of caution here. When we are talking of “improving quality”, “obsession with quality”, “continual improvement”, etc, let’s be sure not only to think in terms of the quality of product or service as received by the customer. … Alongside the quality of what the customer receives, we must be thinking of the quality of what goes into the production and delivery of that product and/or service … Which is what the Deming philosophy is about …

items.proposal: Now, a loud word of caution here. When we are talking of "improving quality", "obsession with quality", "continual improvement", etc, let's be sure not *only* to think in terms of the quality of product or service as received by the customer. That might lead us in the direction, for example, of depending on mass inspection which, as we shall soon see, is in direct contradiction to the third of the 14 Points. Alongside the quality of what the customer receives, we *must* be thinking of the quality of what goes into the *production* and *delivery* of that product and/or service—the processes, the ability and willingness of people and groups within the organisation to work together to solve and indeed prevent problems, and to find and implement better ways of doing things. Attempting to improve quality of product/service *without* those broader considerations may well prove to be impossibly expensive and so lead to a dead end. But, yet again, here we are immediately getting involved with those "unknowable figures" and very much with the whole way in which the organisation is managed. Which is what the Deming philosophy is about …

items.site_html: “A simple equilateral triangle with one short phrase written at each of its three corners …” and the two other <details> blocks.
items.evidence_html: Unsourced 1, 3 and 4. These are the accessibility descriptions for the three Triangle figures, written for the site. Existing by design; workflow/PATTERNS.md requires them. The fourth unsourced flag (Unsourced 2) is not in this category — it is invented prose, handled as D4-39.

items.source_html: Cover page, contents listing with clock timings, and the “(9.00am – 12.45pm; 1.45pm – 5.30pm)” session banner.
items.site_html: Not reproduced.
items.evidence_html: Gaps 1–5 and Altered 3, 22, 25, 33. The PDF's contents page and the letter-prefixed running head (“G DAY 4: …”) are print furniture. The site's equivalent is the book sidebar. Consistent with every prior pass in this wave.

items.source_html: Yellow banners: “Activity 4–a (pages 4–5) is also on Workbook pages 49–50”, and five more.
items.site_html: Not reproduced.
items.evidence_html: Visible on every page image opened for this pass. These point at the separate printed Workbook, which the site does not ship and which has no web counterpart. Omitted site-wide by design — they appear in no day.

items.source_html: “If No … please move on to page 7.”
items.site_html: The If-No branch is given inline, immediately after If-Yes.
items.evidence_html: Short line 3. In print the two branches are on facing pages and the reader is told to turn over; on the site both are on one page, so the instruction has nothing to instruct. The If-No text itself is present and matches printed p7. Deliberate restructuring, not a loss.

items.source_html: “friend/spouse/partner”, “could/should”, “product/service”, “run/control charts”
items.site_html: “friend / spouse / partner”, “could / should”.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed as site-wide rather than local: the spaced form appears across the corpus and is how the site sets tight slashes for readability. A single-instance “convention” would be a defect; this one is not.

items.source_html: “If Yes …” / “If No …” — italic.
items.site_html: “**If Yes …**” / “**If No …**” — bold.
items.evidence_html: Printed p6 image. The site uses bold for branch labels in activities throughout, and the change is a deliberate reading-order cue rather than drift. Left as is.

items.source_html: Printed p14–15: “he often used shorter versions”; the full Out of the Crisis Chapter 2/3 bullet; “I am giving you plenty of help … as the 12 Days go by … rather less”.
items.site_html: All three read exactly as the source does.
items.evidence_html: Re-checked against the printed p14 and p15 page images at the start of this pass. These are #676's three fixes, and they are correctly applied — so this pass proposes nothing on them. The one defect #676 left on those pages is D4-40.

sections.title: Out of scope for a per-day pass
sections.note_html: Real, but the wrong instrument. Recorded so they are handed on rather than quietly dropped.

items.source_html: The day's contents page lists Point 2 on p 18 and Point 4 on p 22.
items.site_html: Neither ## Point 2. The new philosophy (:65) nor ## Point 4. End lowest-tender contracts (:181) carries a {#sec-pageNN} anchor, while Points 1, 3, 5 and 6 all do.
items.evidence_html: A real gap, but it belongs to epic #610's anchor work rather than to a transcription pass — nothing currently links to those two pages, so there is no wrong-destination defect to fix, only a missing future target. Raised here so the next #610 sweep has it. D4-37 is different and stays in scope: that anchor exists, is wrong, and already has two inbound links resolving through it.

items.source_html: The three Joiner Triangle diagrams on printed p2, p11 and p13, and the Scientific Approach box on p12.
items.site_html: Carried as PNGs with <details> descriptions; the box contents are not transcribed as text.
items.evidence_html: Altered 30, 32, 34, 36 and 38 and Gaps 8–11 all reduce to the same thing: the comparator is trying to score a two-column diagram against prose. Whether the boxes' wording is faithful is a real question and the page images suggest it is, but it is #725's instrument, not this one's.
